description: Sample design, query and presentation challenges. Replace or extend with packs generated from your own lectures.

design.title: Riverbend Veterinary Clinic
design.brief:
Riverbend Veterinary Clinic wants a database to keep track of pet owners, their pets, and clinic visits.

For each OWNER the clinic records an owner ID (unique), the owner's name, phone number, and address. The address is made up of a street, a city, and a zip code.

Each owner may have many pets registered at the clinic (though a newly registered owner may not have added a pet yet). Every PET belongs to exactly one owner. For each pet the clinic records a pet ID (unique), the pet's name, its species, and its birth date. The clinic also wants to display the pet's age, which can be calculated from the birth date.

A VISIT is recorded every time a pet is brought in. Each visit has a visit number (unique), a visit date, and notes. A visit is for exactly one pet, and a pet may have many visits or none at all.

The clinic employs VETERINARIANS. Each veterinarian has an employee ID (unique) and a name, and may have one or more specialties (for example, 'surgery' and 'dentistry'). Each visit is handled by exactly one veterinarian; a veterinarian handles many visits, but a newly hired veterinarian may not have handled any yet.
hints: Four entities are named in capitals in the brief.
'Can be calculated' signals a derived attribute; 'one or more specialties' signals a multivalued attribute.
All three relationships are 1:M. Ask on each side: at most one or many? At least zero or one?

relationships.name: Owns
relationships.rationale: Each pet has exactly one owner; an owner may have many pets or none.

relationships.name: BroughtFor
relationships.rationale: A visit is for exactly one pet; a pet may have many visits or none.

relationships.name: Handles
relationships.rationale: Each visit has exactly one veterinarian; a veterinarian may have handled many visits or none.

tables.name: VET_SPECIALTY
tables.note: The multivalued attribute Specialty must become its own table (EmpID + Specialty).

notes: Age is derived, so it is not stored. The composite Address becomes Street, City, Zip.

design.title: Campus Events Office
design.brief:
The Campus Events Office needs a database for student organizations and the events they run.

Each STUDENT has a student ID (unique), a name, an email address, and a major.

Each ORGANIZATION has an org ID (unique), a name, and a type (academic, social, service, ...). Every organization has exactly one president, who is a student; a student can be president of at most one organization, and most students are not presidents of anything.

Students join organizations: a student can be a member of many organizations or none, and an organization can have many student members (a brand-new organization may have none yet).

Each EVENT has an event ID (unique), a title, a date, and a capacity. Every event is sponsored by exactly one organization; an organization may sponsor many events or none.

Each event takes place at exactly one VENUE. A venue has a venue ID (unique), a name, and a building. A venue may host many events over time or none.

Students register for events. A student may register for many events (or none), and an event may have many registered students (or none). For each registration the office records the registration date and whether the student actually attended.
hints: There are two M:N relationships and one of them carries attributes.
'Exactly one president ... at most one organization' describes a 1:1 relationship with different participation on each side.
In the relational schema, a 1:1 relationship becomes a foreign key on one side. Which side has mandatory participation?

relationships.name: Presides
relationships.rationale: Every organization has exactly one president (mandatory, 1); a student presides over at most one organization (optional, 1).

relationships.name: Sponsors
relationships.rationale: Each event has exactly one sponsoring organization; an organization sponsors many events or none.

relationships.name: HeldAt
relationships.rationale: Each event is at exactly one venue; a venue hosts many events or none.

relationships.name: RegistersFor
relationships.rationale: Many-to-many with attributes; the attributes belong to the relationship.

tables.name: MEMBERSHIP
tables.note: The M:N MemberOf relationship needs a bridge table.

tables.name: REGISTRATION
tables.note: The M:N RegistersFor relationship needs a bridge table that also holds RegDate and Attended.

notes: For the 1:1 Presides relationship, the foreign key belongs on ORGANIZATION (mandatory side): every organization has a president, but most students do not preside over anything, so a PresidentOf column in STUDENT would be mostly NULL.

design.title: Riverbend Rentals
design.brief:
Riverbend Cycles is launching a bike rental service and needs a database.

Each rental BIKE has a bike ID (unique), a model, a type (road, trail, e-bike, ...), and an hourly rate.

A CUSTOMER has a customer ID (unique), a name, an email address, and one or more phone numbers.

Rental STATIONS have a station ID (unique), a station name, and a location consisting of a street and a city.

A RENTAL has a rental ID (unique), a start time, an end time, and a total cost that is computed from the duration and the bike's hourly rate. Every rental is made by exactly one customer and involves exactly one bike; customers and bikes may have many rentals or none. Every rental is picked up at exactly one station. A rental may be returned to a station (any station), but an in-progress rental has no return station yet. A station may be the pick-up point for many rentals and the return point for many rentals.

Maintenance work on bikes must be logged. Each MAINTENANCE LOG entry has a log number, a date, and a description. Log numbers restart at 1 for each bike, so a log entry can only be identified together with its bike. Each log entry belongs to exactly one bike; a bike may have many log entries or none.

Each EMPLOYEE has an employee ID (unique) and a name, works at exactly one station, and may supervise other employees. Each employee has at most one supervisor, and some employees (managers) have none. A station has many employees or none (a station being set up).
hints: 'Can only be identified together with its bike' is the definition of a weak entity with a partial key and an identifying relationship.
Two different relationships connect STATION and RENTAL (pick-up and return). Give them different names.
'May supervise other employees' is a unary (recursive) 1:M relationship on EMPLOYEE.
In the schema, RENTAL needs two foreign keys to STATION with different column names.

relationships.name: Rents
relationships.rationale: Every rental is by exactly one customer; a customer may have many rentals or none.

relationships.name: Involves
relationships.rationale: Every rental involves exactly one bike; a bike may be in many rentals or none.

relationships.name: PickedUpAt
relationships.rationale: Every rental has exactly one pick-up station.

relationships.name: ReturnedTo
relationships.rationale: A rental has at most one return station, and none while in progress: optional on the station side.

relationships.name: Has
relationships.rationale: Identifying relationship: every log entry belongs to exactly one bike.

relationships.name: WorksAt
relationships.rationale: Each employee works at exactly one station; a station has many employees or none.

relationships.name: Supervises
relationships.rationale: Unary 1:M: an employee has at most one supervisor (optional); a supervisor may supervise many employees.

tables.name: CUSTOMER_PHONE
tables.note: The multivalued Phone attribute becomes its own table.

tables.name: MAINTENANCE_LOG
tables.note: Weak entity: its PK is the owner's key plus the partial key.

notes: TotalCost is derived and not stored.
ReturnStationID and SupervisorID must allow NULL.

questions.text: List the name and price of every product.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Product

questions.text: Show every column of every store.
questions.sql: SELECT * FROM Store

questions.text: List the first name, last name, and city of every customer.
questions.sql: SELECT FirstName, LastName, City FROM Customer

questions.text: List the names of products priced above ${{price}}.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName FROM Product WHERE Price > {{price}}

questions.text: List the first and last names of customers who live in the state {{state}}.
questions.sql: SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Customer WHERE State = '{{state}}'

questions.text: List the product ID and name of products in category {{cat}} that cost less than ${{price}}.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductID, ProductName FROM Product WHERE CategoryID = '{{cat}}' AND Price < {{price}}
hints: Combine two conditions with AND.

questions.text: List the distinct cities where customers live, in alphabetical order.
questions.sql: SELECT DISTINCT City FROM Customer ORDER BY City
hints: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows; ORDER BY sorts.

questions.text: List every product name and price, most expensive first.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Product ORDER BY Price DESC

questions.text: List the distinct states in which the company has customers.
questions.sql: SELECT DISTINCT State FROM Customer

questions.text: List the names and prices of products whose name contains the word '{{word}}'.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Product WHERE ProductName LIKE '%{{word}}%'
hints: LIKE with % wildcards on both sides.

questions.text: List the transaction ID and date of all transactions that took place in {{month}} (given as YYYY-MM).
questions.sql: SELECT TID, TDate FROM SalesTransaction WHERE TMonth = '{{month}}'
hints: TMonth stores the month as text, or use LIKE on TDate.

questions.text: List the names of products priced between ${{lo}} and ${{hi}} inclusive.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName FROM Product WHERE Price BETWEEN {{lo}} AND {{hi}}

questions.text: List the last names and states of customers who live in either {{s1}} or {{s2}}.
questions.sql: SELECT LastName, State FROM Customer WHERE State IN ('{{s1}}', '{{s2}}')

questions.text: How many products are in the catalog? Return a single number.
questions.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Product

questions.text: What are the highest and the lowest product prices? Return both in one row.
questions.sql: SELECT MAX(Price), MIN(Price) FROM Product

questions.text: What is the average price of the products supplied by vendor {{vid}}? Round to 2 decimals.
questions.sql: SELECT ROUND(AVG(Price), 2) FROM Product WHERE VendorID = '{{vid}}'

questions.text: What is the total quantity of product {{pid}} ever sold? Return a single number.
questions.sql: SELECT SUM(Quantity) FROM SoldVia WHERE ProductID = '{{pid}}'

questions.text: For each category ID, show the category ID and the number of products in it.
questions.sql: SELECT CategoryID, COUNT(*) FROM Product GROUP BY CategoryID

questions.text: For each store ID, show the store ID and the number of transactions made there (only stores with transactions).
questions.sql: SELECT StoreID, COUNT(*) FROM SalesTransaction GROUP BY StoreID

questions.text: For each product ID, show the product ID and the total quantity sold.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductID, SUM(Quantity) FROM SoldVia GROUP BY ProductID

questions.text: Show total revenue per month: the month (YYYY-MM) and the sum of LineTotal, sorted chronologically.
questions.sql: SELECT TMonth, SUM(LineTotal) FROM SalesTransaction T JOIN SoldVia S ON T.TID = S.TID GROUP BY TMonth ORDER BY TMonth
hints: Join SalesTransaction to SoldVia, group by TMonth.

questions.text: Show the category IDs that have more than {{n}} products, with the product count.
questions.sql: SELECT CategoryID, COUNT(*) FROM Product GROUP BY CategoryID HAVING COUNT(*) > {{n}}
hints: Conditions on aggregates go in HAVING, not WHERE.

questions.text: Show the product IDs with a total quantity sold greater than {{n}}, with the total.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductID, SUM(Quantity) FROM SoldVia GROUP BY ProductID HAVING SUM(Quantity) > {{n}}

questions.text: Show the customer IDs of customers who made at least {{n}} transactions, with their transaction count.
questions.sql: SELECT CustomerID, COUNT(*) FROM SalesTransaction GROUP BY CustomerID HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{n}}

questions.text: List each product's name together with its category name.
questions.sql: SELECT P.ProductName, C.CategoryName FROM Product P JOIN Category C ON P.CategoryID = C.CategoryID

questions.text: List the product name and vendor name for every product supplied by a vendor from {{country}}.
questions.sql: SELECT P.ProductName, V.VendorName FROM Product P JOIN Vendor V ON P.VendorID = V.VendorID WHERE V.Country = '{{country}}'

questions.text: List the store name and transaction date of every transaction made by customer {{cid}}.
questions.sql: SELECT S.StoreName, T.TDate FROM SalesTransaction T JOIN Store S ON T.StoreID = S.StoreID WHERE T.CustomerID = '{{cid}}'

questions.text: For every transaction, show the transaction ID, the customer's last name, and the store name.
questions.sql: SELECT T.TID, C.LastName, S.StoreName FROM SalesTransaction T JOIN Customer C ON T.CustomerID = C.CustomerID JOIN Store S ON T.StoreID = S.StoreID

questions.text: Show the product name and quantity for every line of transaction {{tid}}.
questions.sql: SELECT P.ProductName, S.Quantity FROM SoldVia S JOIN Product P ON S.ProductID = P.ProductID WHERE S.TID = '{{tid}}'

questions.text: For each category name, show the total revenue (sum of LineTotal).
questions.sql: SELECT C.CategoryName, SUM(S.LineTotal) FROM SoldVia S JOIN Product P ON S.ProductID = P.ProductID JOIN Category C ON P.CategoryID = C.CategoryID GROUP BY C.CategoryName
hints: Three tables: SoldVia → Product → Category.

questions.text: For each region name, show the number of transactions made in stores of that region.
questions.sql: SELECT R.RegionName, COUNT(*) FROM SalesTransaction T JOIN Store S ON T.StoreID = S.StoreID JOIN Region R ON S.RegionID = R.RegionID GROUP BY R.RegionName

questions.text: For each customer who made more than {{n}} transactions, show first name, last name, and the number of transactions.
questions.sql: SELECT C.FirstName, C.LastName, COUNT(*) FROM SalesTransaction T JOIN Customer C ON T.CustomerID = C.CustomerID GROUP BY C.CustomerID, C.FirstName, C.LastName HAVING COUNT(*) > {{n}}

questions.text: List each product name and its price after a 20% discount, for products priced over ${{price}}. Label the discounted price however you like.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName, Price * 0.8 AS SalePrice FROM Product WHERE Price > {{price}}

questions.text: List the names of products that have never been sold.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName FROM Product WHERE ProductID NOT IN (SELECT ProductID FROM SoldVia)
hints: NOT IN with a subquery over SoldVia.

questions.text: List the name and price of products priced above the average product price.
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName, Price FROM Product WHERE Price > (SELECT AVG(Price) FROM Product)

questions.text: List the first and last names of customers who have made at least one purchase at store {{sid}}.
questions.sql: SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Customer WHERE CustomerID IN (SELECT CustomerID FROM SalesTransaction WHERE StoreID = '{{sid}}')

questions.text: List the name(s) of the most expensive product(s).
questions.sql: SELECT ProductName FROM Product WHERE Price = (SELECT MAX(Price) FROM Product)

questions.text: List, in one column and without duplicates, every city that is either a customer's city or a store's city.
questions.sql: SELECT City FROM Customer UNION SELECT City FROM Store
hints: UNION removes duplicates automatically.

questions.text: List the cities that are both a customer's city and a store's city.
questions.sql: SELECT City FROM Customer INTERSECT SELECT City FROM Store

questions.text: List the cities where customers live but where there is no store.
questions.sql: SELECT City FROM Customer EXCEPT SELECT City FROM Store
hints: Oracle calls it MINUS; SQLite calls it EXCEPT.

questions.text: List the vendor names that supply at least one product in the category named '{{catname}}'.
questions.sql: SELECT VendorName FROM Vendor V WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Product P JOIN Category C ON P.CategoryID = C.CategoryID WHERE P.VendorID = V.VendorID AND C.CategoryName = '{{catname}}')

questions.text: List every store name with its number of transactions, including stores with zero transactions.
questions.sql: SELECT S.StoreName, COUNT(T.TID) FROM Store S LEFT JOIN SalesTransaction T ON S.StoreID = T.StoreID GROUP BY S.StoreID, S.StoreName
hints: LEFT JOIN keeps stores without matches; COUNT a column from the right table so the count is 0, not 1.

questions.text: List the first and last names of customers whose zip code is missing.
questions.sql: SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Customer WHERE Zip IS NULL
hints: Use IS NULL, never = NULL.

questions.text: How many customers have a zip code on file? Return a single number.
questions.sql: SELECT COUNT(Zip) FROM Customer

presentation.title: Total revenue
presentation.brief: The owner wants one big number on the dashboard: total revenue across all stores and all time. Build a visual that shows just that number.
hints: A card shows a single value.
Revenue is LineTotal in SoldVia, summed.

presentation.title: Revenue by category
presentation.brief: Which product categories bring in the most money? Show total revenue for each category name, ordered from highest to lowest, with a descriptive title.
hints: Categories are unordered, so a bar or column chart fits.
Use the category NAME, not the ID.
presentation.referenceSql: SELECT C.CategoryName, SUM(S.LineTotal) FROM SoldVia S JOIN Product P ON S.ProductID = P.ProductID JOIN Category C ON P.CategoryID = C.CategoryID GROUP BY C.CategoryName ORDER BY 2 DESC

presentation.title: Monthly revenue trend
presentation.brief: How has revenue developed month by month over the two years? Show the trend of total revenue per month (TMonth), in chronological order, with a title.
hints: Time on the axis calls for a line chart.
Sort by the axis, not by the value.
presentation.referenceSql: SELECT T.TMonth, SUM(S.LineTotal) FROM SalesTransaction T JOIN SoldVia S ON T.TID = S.TID GROUP BY T.TMonth ORDER BY 1

presentation.title: Transactions per store in the West
presentation.brief: The West regional manager wants to compare her stores. Show the number of transactions for each store name, but only for stores in the West region. Add a title.
hints: Filter on RegionName rather than picking store names by hand.
Count transactions (TID).
presentation.referenceSql: SELECT S.StoreName, COUNT(T.TID) FROM SalesTransaction T JOIN Store S ON T.StoreID = S.StoreID JOIN Region R ON S.RegionID = R.RegionID WHERE R.RegionName = 'West' GROUP BY S.StoreName ORDER BY 2 DESC

presentation.title: Share of units by vendor
presentation.brief: Purchasing wants to see what share of all units sold comes from each vendor (by vendor name), as parts of a whole. Give it a title.
hints: 'Share of a whole' with a handful of categories suits a pie or donut.
Units are Quantity in SoldVia.
presentation.referenceSql: SELECT V.VendorName, SUM(S.Quantity) FROM SoldVia S JOIN Product P ON S.ProductID = P.ProductID JOIN Vendor V ON P.VendorID = V.VendorID GROUP BY V.VendorName ORDER BY 2 DESC

presentation.title: Units sold by product
presentation.brief: Which products move the most units? Show total quantity sold for every product name, from most to least sold, with a title. Pick a visual that stays readable with thirty products.
hints: Thirty categories is far too many for a pie.
Horizontal bars keep long product names readable.
presentation.referenceSql: SELECT P.ProductName, SUM(S.Quantity) FROM SoldVia S JOIN Product P ON S.ProductID = P.ProductID GROUP BY P.ProductName ORDER BY 2 DESC

presentation.title: Category revenue by region
presentation.brief: Do the regions buy different things? Compare total revenue per category name, broken down by region name, in a single visual with a title.
hints: Category on the axis, region in the legend.
Revenue is the sum of LineTotal.
presentation.referenceSql: SELECT C.CategoryName, R.RegionName, SUM(S.LineTotal) FROM SoldVia S JOIN Product P ON S.ProductID = P.ProductID JOIN Category C ON P.CategoryID = C.CategoryID JOIN SalesTransaction T ON S.TID = T.TID JOIN Store St ON T.StoreID = St.StoreID JOIN Region R ON St.RegionID = R.RegionID GROUP BY C.CategoryName, R.RegionName ORDER BY 3 DESC

presentation.title: Product revenue table
presentation.brief: Finance wants exact figures, not a picture: a table listing each product name, its category name, and its total revenue, sorted by revenue from high to low.
hints: A table visual; leave the names unsummarized and sum LineTotal.
Sort by the value.
presentation.referenceSql: SELECT P.ProductName, C.CategoryName, SUM(S.LineTotal) FROM SoldVia S JOIN Product P ON S.ProductID = P.ProductID JOIN Category C ON P.CategoryID = C.CategoryID GROUP BY P.ProductName, C.CategoryName ORDER BY 3 DESC
